questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/4ae6f37660956d6d7015289c4a185c12ef4ab39f84e9cff394f534b14854c5cd.png)

The sides of a square are decreasing in length at a rate of $3\text{ m/min}.$ At what rate is the area of ​​the square decreasing when the side is $12\,\text{m}$ long?

The area is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{m}}^{2}/\text{min}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is decreasing at a rate of $3\,\text{m/min},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-3.$ Also, when the sides are $12\,\text{m},$ we have $x=12.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-3\cdot 2(12)=-72{\text{ m}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square is decreasing at $72\,{\text{m}}^{2}/\text{min}.$

questions.problem:
The sides (in meters) of a square are decreasing. At a particular moment, the rate of decrease of the area of the square is numerically equal to twelve times the rate of decrease of the sides. What is the area $A$ of the square at that moment?

$A=$
{{field-1}}${\text{ m}}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=12\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ So, substituting $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}12\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2x\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ 12\cdot \cancel{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}} & =2x\cdot \cancel{\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}} \\ 12 & =2x \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, at that particular moment, we have $x=6\text{ m}$ and the area of the square is

$$
A={6}^{2}=36{\text{ m}}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/eb0c6490a6e587b0d20b10a281584748d9367f2aa53a09159f6703cacbb632bb.png)

If the diagonals of a square increase at a rate of $9\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}\text{/s}$, at what rate is the perimeter changing?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $p$ be the perimeter of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $p$ and $h$ is

$$
p=2\sqrt{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each diagonal of the square is increasing at a rate of $9\sqrt{2}\text{ cm}\text{/s},$ so we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=9\sqrt{2}.
$$

Substituting this information into the above expression for $\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =(9\sqrt{2})\cdot (2\sqrt{2})=36\text{ cm/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the perimeter of the square increases at $36\text{ cm}/\text{s}.$

questions.problem: The sides (in feet) of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to four times the rate of increase of the diagonals. What is the length of the diagonals of the square at that moment?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=4\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$, so replacing $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 4\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 4 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So at that particular moment, we have that the length of the diagonals of the square is $4\text{ feet}.$

questions.problem:
The sides (in centimeters) of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to eight times the rate of increase of the diagonal. What is the area $A$ of the square at that moment?

$A=$
{{field-1}} ${\text{cm}}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that
$\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=8\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t},$
so replacing $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}8\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 8\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 8 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So, at that particular moment, we have $h=8,$ and therefore the area of the square at that moment is

$$
A=\frac{(8)^{2}}{2}=\frac{64}{2}=32\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Each side of a square is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/min}.$ How fast is the area of the square decreasing when the sides are $10\,\text{cm}?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/a06eb0963dc6d01e45acb9349e5232ba70a11c98c99ee63c2ec0dae3d748f5ed.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} .
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A = x^2.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is decreasing at a rate of $2\,\text{cm/min},$ so we have $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t} = -2.$ Also, when the sides are $10\,\text{cm},$ we have $x=10.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =(-2)\cdot 2(10)=-40{\text{ cm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square decreases at a rate of $40\,\text{cm}^2/\text{min}.$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
This situation is different. Here, the *area* is changing at a constant rate,  and we want to know the rate at which the side lengths are changing.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14095797/assets/f4125cebd7553bb8b106a8baff39a6e4a120b9d9e5cdf2c4c9c0a9a676558897.png)

We want to find $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d t}.$ The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A = x^2.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x\end{aligned}
$$

We know from the given information that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =-20\text{ cm[math]^2[/math]/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this information, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}-20 & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{10}{x}.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A = \dfrac{h^2}{2}.
$$

Using implicit differentiation and the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm d t} = 2\dfrac{\textrm d h}{\textrm d t}$, so replacing $\dfrac{\textrm d A}{\textrm dt}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 2\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 2 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So at that particular moment, we have $h=2,$ and therefore the area of the square at that moment is

$$
